title: Chapter XIX

teacherSummary.text: Collins proposes to Elizabeth with a speech listing reasons, including Lady Catherine's advice. She refuses; he insists that elegant ladies always refuse at first and that she may never get another offer.

context.history: A woman refusing a secure match was risky; Collins's offer would have saved her home.

significance: Elizabeth's refusal asserts the right to marry for affection and respect.
discussionQuestions: Why does Elizabeth refuse, even though marrying Collins would secure her family's home?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XIX,” how does Austen show a ridiculous proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIX develops the idea of a ridiculous proposal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XIX to complicate the reader's understanding of a ridiculous proposal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a ridiculous proposal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a ridiculous proposal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “Upon my word, Sir,” cried Elizabeth, “your hope is rather an extraordinary one after my declaration. I do assure you that I am not one of those young ladies (if such young ladies there are) who are so daring as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who would make you so. Nay, were your friend Lady Catherine to know me, I am persuaded she would find me in every respect ill qualified for the situation.”

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Elizabeth refuse, even though marrying Collins would secure her family's home? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include dissemble, singled, sanctioned, disapprove, footstool. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “You can hardly doubt the purport of my discourse, however your natural delicacy may lead you to dissemble; my attentions have been too marked to be mistaken.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To hide under a false semblance or seeming.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. A woman refusing a secure match was risky; Collins's offer would have saved her home. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's refusal asserts the right to marry for affection and respect. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot irony, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
